At the park, Faith Allen of Madison Heights stood with a "Dump Trump” sign.

“I don’t like any of Trump’s policies," Allen said. "He scares me. I don’t like all the connections with Russia that’s been coming out. I don’t like him tweeting." She said she thinks he's paranoid.

The rallies for Trump were held nationwide as a counterpoint to protest demonstrations that have grown since his inauguration, ranging from the millions of people who participated in Women’s Marches across the state and nation to raucous town hall meetings with Republican members of Congress in recent weeks.

Macomb County, where Freedom Hill is located, was an especially fertile place for this weekend’s so-called flash mobs. The birthplace of the Reagan Democrats voted twice for President Barack Obama, giving the Democrat significant winning margins in both 2008 and 2012. But in 2016, things reversed, with the Republican Trump getting 53.6% of the vote in Macomb compared with 42.1% for Democrat Hillary Clinton. Trump ended up winning Michigan — the first time a Republican has won the state since 1988 — by a 10,704-vote margin.

Supporters of Trump held several flash mobs across the state before the Nov. 8 election to drum up enthusiasm — and votes — for the controversial New York businessman.

In Lansing on Saturday, event coordinator Meshawn Maddock said several hundred Trump supporters converged on the state capitol, as well as some counter-protesters. She said there were no problems.

“I’m thrilled," Maddock said afterward about how things went. "I wish Trump could see it. …It’s a great way for both sides to show their feelings."

She said she hoped the events would be energizing for supporters of the president in the face of opposition.

"I think a lot of Trump supporters feel like we can’t take our foot off the gas,” she said.

Rallies also were scheduled Saturday in Bloomfield Hills, Grand Rapids, Antrim County, Emmet County and Grand Traverse County.

About 30 opponents of abortion restrictions rallied in Jacksonville’s Hemming Park on Monday and urged state lawmakers to increase access to reproductive medical services.

“We don’t want any more restrictive bills,” said organizer Christina Kittle from the group Coalition for Consent, who told demonstrators to celebrate the fact that proposals to restrict abortion access all stalled in this year Florida’s Legislature session.

Gathered in the public space that City Hall faces, speakers warned that abortion restrictions proposed elsewhere would threaten women’s medical privacy and autonomy.

“This is bigger than abortion. This is bigger than reproductive rights. They’re going after the right to privacy,” Lanelle Phillmon, a Navy retiree, told the crowd, which chanted messages such as “Our body, our choice,” and “No more restrictions; my body is not your jurisdiction.”

Kittle, who called out support by state Rep. Kimberly Daniels, D-Jacksonville, for legislation requiring parental consent for a minor to have an abortion, told demonstrators to encourage steps to increase access, such as a bill by Sen. Lauren Book, D-Plantation, that would have required hospital emergency rooms to make information on “morning after” contraception available to sex assault victims.

Three counter-demonstrators held signs aloft or answered speakers with arguments of their own.

“You guys are hypocrites,” 21-year-old Michael Cotter of Jacksonville told the rally group. “Why does the baby deserve to die for another person’s decision?”

Jordyn Crippen, another Jacksonville millennial, carried a black sign with a drawing of a fetus and the words “Human Rights.” She said she learned of the rally on Facebook and decided to attend because she believed pro-choice arguments don’t recognize the value of unborn lives.

At least a dozen police officers with bikes, golf carts and video cameras hovered around the gathering, talking with people on both sides.

Although a police loudspeaker projected a message before the rally emphasizing respect for demonstrator rights, neither side of the gathering was allowed to do the same.

The city’s noise ordinance limited sounds from gatherings in public places like Hemming Park to 60 decibels, Michael Williams, a branch manager with the city’s environmental agency, told demonstrators before the rally cranked up. That meant people could shout and cup their hands, he told the crowd, but no one could use a bullhorn or a public address speaker.

“Either side,” Williams said, “it doesn’t matter to us.”
